title: Strait of Hormuz: U.S. Makes Progress, But Iran War Drags On
summary:
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway through which about one-fifth of the world's traded oil and gas passes in peacetime. In February, the U.S. and Israel launched a war against Iran, expecting it to last a few weeks. Iran retaliated by effectively closing the strait, causing a global economic shock. Now, months later, the U.S. has made progress in reopening the route, but the war is far from over.

A U.S. blockade has virtually halted Iran's oil exports, which dropped from 1.85 million barrels a day last spring to around 255,000 in August, according to Kpler, a global trade monitor. Meanwhile, exports of non-Iranian oil through the strait rose from 300,000 barrels a day at the height of the war to 10.8 million in September. U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said, "we're probably two-thirds or more of preconflict flows." Before the war, non-Iranian exports were about 14 million barrels a day.

But the increased flow depends on a major U.S. military deployment that has strained resources. The war has cost U.S. taxpayers more than $37.5 billion and left 18 U.S. service members dead. It is also expected to hurt Republicans in November's midterm elections. President Trump has acknowledged that gas prices are likely to stay high through the elections.

Iran's economy is suffering under the blockade and new sanctions, with rising prices and long lines at gas stations. Yet Iran shows no sign of backing down. "Tehran has repeatedly signaled that it will respond to growing U.S. pressure by moving up the escalation ladder, not by backing down," wrote Danny Citrinowicz, a former Israeli intelligence officer. Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen have stepped up attacks on Saudi oil facilities, helping push the price of Brent crude above $100 a barrel this week. Diesel hit a record high, potentially fueling inflation.

Experts say the war is a stalemate. "Washington's main problem is that it still lacks a theory of victory," said Ali Vaez of the International Crisis Group. "More ships are getting through, and Iran is hurting, yet none of that has produced a political outcome." With no diplomatic progress since a June agreement crumbled, the conflict looks set to continue.
why_it_matters: Oil prices set at a faraway chokepoint reach teenagers through bus fares, grocery bills, and family budgets, and the article shows how hard it is for even the most powerful country to turn military force into a political result — a lesson about the limits of power that today's students will inherit as voters.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz (the narrow channel between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula that connects the Persian Gulf to the open ocean) has been a flashpoint for decades. In the 1980s, during the long Iran-Iraq war, both countries attacked oil tankers there in what became known as the 'Tanker War,' and the U.S. Navy escorted Kuwaiti ships so that oil could keep moving.

In 2015, Iran signed a nuclear deal with world powers known as the JCPOA, accepting limits on its nuclear program in exchange for relief from tough economic sanctions. The United States withdrew from that deal in 2018 and reimposed sanctions, part of the long standoff the article describes.

Brent crude (a benchmark price for oil from the North Sea that traders use to set prices worldwide) rises when ships cannot move freely through chokepoints, and higher oil prices eventually show up in what families pay for fuel, food, and transport.

Kpler (a private company that tracks ships and global trade flows) is the kind of monitor journalists use for exact export numbers. The Houthis (a movement that controls much of northern Yemen and has fought a long civil war there) have attacked Saudi oil sites before, which is why their role in pushing prices up matters here.

OPEN QUESTION: no diplomatic progress since a June agreement crumbled — how does this war end?

perspectives.description: From this angle the story is progress: the blockade has cut Iran's oil exports dramatically while non-Iranian shipping has climbed back to roughly two-thirds of prewar levels. More tankers getting through means less pressure on global fuel supplies and, eventually, some relief on prices.

perspectives.perspective: Critics of the war and cost-conscious taxpayers (critical)
perspectives.description: This view stresses the bill: more than $37.5 billion spent, 18 service members dead, and no clear end point. Critics argue the deployment strains U.S. resources, gas prices stay high for voters, and the expected midterm backlash shows a war being fought without a stated definition of victory.

Analysts like Ali Vaez frame this as a classic stalemate: both sides are being hurt, ships are moving, yet no political outcome has been produced. Historically, blockades and chokepoint fights — including the 1980s Tanker War — rarely force a government to surrender its goals; they mostly raise costs on everyone.

With a June agreement collapsed and Iran signaling it will climb the 'escalation ladder' rather than back down, this angle asks what a negotiated off-ramp could look like. It also warns that proxy attacks by Iran's allies could widen the conflict and keep energy prices volatile for months.
